A. Most Likely Diagnosis

β-thalassaemia major (homozygous β0 / β+ thalassaemia) — also called Cooley's anaemia or Mediterranean anaemia. The clinical picture of early-infancy onset severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia in a child of consanguineous parents, with typical facial and skeletal changes, hepatosplenomegaly, and transfusion dependence from 6 months of age is classical.

B. Etiopathogenesis

β-thalassaemias are inherited disorders of haemoglobin synthesis caused by reduced (β+) or absent (β0) synthesis of the β-globin chain of adult haemoglobin (HbA = α2β2). The β-globin gene cluster is on chromosome 11p15.5.

Molecular Basis

  • >300 mutations described — point mutations (most common), small deletions, splice-site defects, promoter mutations.
  • Inheritance — autosomal recessive; homozygous or compound heterozygous state produces clinical disease; heterozygotes (thalassaemia minor / trait) are asymptomatic carriers with mild microcytosis.
  • Common Indian mutations — IVS 1-5 (G→C), Codon 8/9 (+G), Codon 41/42 (-TCTT), 619 bp deletion at 3' end.

Pathophysiology

  • Defective β-chain synthesis → reduced HbA production.
  • Excess unpaired α-chains precipitate in red-cell precursors → oxidative damage → ineffective erythropoiesis (intramedullary death of erythroid precursors) and haemolysis of circulating RBCs.
  • Result — severe anaemia, compensatory erythroid hyperplasia in marrow and extramedullary sites, iron overload from transfusions & increased gut absorption (hepcidin suppression).
  • Unpaired γ-chains form Hb Bart's (in fetus) and HbF (in adult) — increased HbF is a compensatory mechanism; γ-chain persistence modifies severity.

C. Peripheral Smear & Bone Marrow Findings

Peripheral Blood Smear

  • Severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia — Hb 4–7 g/dL, MCV 50–60 fL, MCH 12–18 pg.
  • Poikilocytosis — target cells, tear-drop cells, schistocytes, basophilic stippling.
  • Nucleated red cells (orthochromic normoblasts) — numerous.
  • Polychromasia, anisocytosis, basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies, Pappenheimer bodies (siderotic granules).
  • Leukocytosis & thrombocytosis (reactive, due to erythroid hyperplasia).
  • Reticulocyte count — low relative to anaemia (ineffective erythropoiesis).
  • Presence of α-chain precipitation bodies (Heinz body-like) after supravital staining.

Bone Marrow

  • Hypercellular marrow with marked erythroid hyperplasia (M:E ratio reversed, 1:10 or 1:20 vs normal 3:1).
  • Abnormal erythroid precursors — nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony, megaloblastoid changes, basophilic stippling, α-chain inclusions, karyorrhexis, "coronet" cells.
  • Iron stores markedly increased (sideroblasts & ringed sideroblasts).
  • Plasma cells, mast cells often increased.

D. Pathogenesis of Skeletal Deformities & Hepatosplenomegaly

Skeletal Deformities

  • Severe anaemia → tissue hypoxia → erythropoietin release → massive erythroid hyperplasia of marrow.
  • Marrow cavities expand → thinning of cortical bone, bossing of skull ("hair-on-end" appearance on X-ray — Crewcut skull), frontal bossing, maxillary prominence (rodent facies), malocclusion, dental caries.
  • Long bones — widened metaphyses, "Erlenmeyer flask" deformity of distal femur, pathological fractures.
  • Vertebral compression, deformities, osteoporosis, growth retardation, short stature.
  • Extramedullary haematopoiesis — paravertebral masses in thorax (visible on imaging).
  • Facial deformities & malocclusion — typical "chipmunk facies" in untreated children.

Hepatosplenomegaly

  • Extramedullary haematopoiesis in liver & spleen.
  • Haemolysis of abnormal RBCs → increased workload of reticuloendothelial system → Kupffer cell & splenic macrophage hyperplasia.
  • Iron overload from transfusions & increased GI absorption → hepatic fibrosis, eventually cirrhosis.
  • Splenomegaly worsens — hypersplenism → pancytopenia → worsening anaemia, requiring splenectomy.

E. Laboratory Investigations to Confirm Diagnosis

  1. Hb electrophoresis / HPLC — reduced or absent HbA; markedly increased HbF (10–95%), increased HbA2 (in carriers, not always in homozygotes due to γ-chain persistence).
  2. Complete blood count with peripheral smear — microcytic hypochromic anaemia with characteristic morphology.
  3. Reticulocyte count — inappropriately low for degree of anaemia.
  4. Iron studies — high serum iron, ferritin (pre-existing transfusional iron overload), high transferrin saturation.
  5. Serum bilirubin (indirect), LDH, haptoglobin — haemolysis parameters.
  6. Molecular studies — ARMS-PCR, reverse dot blot, DNA sequencing of β-globin gene; identifies specific mutation for genetic counselling & prenatal diagnosis.
  7. Prenatal diagnosis — chorionic villus sampling at 10–12 weeks; PCR-based mutation analysis of fetal DNA.
  8. Parental screening — Hb electrophoresis of both parents (high HbA2 >3.5% indicates β-thal trait).
  9. Imaging — skull & long-bone X-rays (hair-on-end skull, expanded marrow), ultrasound hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac MRI T2* for iron load, DEXA for bone density.
  10. Endocrine workup — glucose tolerance, thyroid, calcium, growth hormone, pubertal status (iron overload complications).

F. Complications of Repeated Transfusions & Disease

Transfusion-related

  • Iron overload — each unit of PRBC contains 200 mg iron; without chelation, iron accumulates in heart (dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias — leading cause of death), liver (fibrosis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma), endocrine glands (growth retardation, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), skin (bronze hyperpigmentation).
  • Transfusion-transmitted infections — HBV, HCV, HIV, malaria, syphilis, TT virus; screened but residual risk persists.
  • Alloimmunisation — anti-Rh, Kell, Duffy; complicates cross-matching.
  • Febrile non-haemolytic, allergic, anaphylactic reactions; TRALI, TACO; acute haemolytic reactions (clerical error).
  • Post-transfusion graft-vs-host disease — irradiate cellular components.

Disease-related

  • Growth retardation, delayed puberty, hypogonadism.
  • Skeletal deformities, pathological fractures, osteoporosis.
  • Splenomegaly → hypersplenism → pancytopenia; many require splenectomy (with pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccination & penicillin prophylaxis).
  • Gallstones (pigment) — chronic haemolysis.
  • Chronic leg ulcers.
  • Pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure.
  • Thrombosis — especially after splenectomy (post-splenectomy thrombocytosis).
  • Hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC.
  • Endocrinopathies — diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism.
  • Psychosocial issues — school absenteeism, depression, financial burden.
  • Acute transformation — parvovirus B19 infection causes transient red-cell aplasia ("aplastic crisis").

Clinical Pearl

Three pillars of management — (1) regular transfusion to keep Hb >9–10 g/dL (suppresses marrow hyperplasia & skeletal changes), (2) iron chelation (deferasirox, deferiprone, deferoxamine) starting after 10–20 transfusions, (3) curative haematopoietic stem-cell transplant from HLA-matched sibling. Gene therapy (betibeglogene autotemcel — lovo-cel) is now approved for transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia.

A. Most Likely Diagnosis

Pulmonary tuberculosis — secondary (post-primary) TB with right upper lobe cavity. The combination of chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum, evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, contact history, characteristic upper-lobe cavity on chest X-ray, and AFB-positive sputum is classical for reactivation pulmonary TB.

B. Etiopathogenesis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis — acid-fast, aerobic, slow-growing (12–24 h division time) intracellular bacillus. Transmission by inhalation of droplet nuclei (1–5 µm) generated by coughing/sneezing of an infectious patient. Risk factors include close contact, malnutrition, immunosuppression (HIV, anti-TNF, steroids, diabetes, silicosis), smoking, crowded living conditions.

Pathogenesis Sequence

  1. Inhalation → alveolar macrophage phagocytosis; bacilli resist killing via sulfatides, lipoarabinomannan (LAM), cord factor (trehalose dimycolate). Multiply within macrophages, spread to regional hilar lymph nodes.
  2. Primary infection (Ghon complex) — subpleural focus (lower lobe / apical segment of upper lobe) + draining hilar lymph node granuloma. Usually asymptomatic; heals with calcification in 90% of immunocompetent adults.
  3. Latent TB infection (LTBI) — dormant bacilli in apices of upper lobe (high O2 tension, "Simon focus"); lifelong in 90% of infected individuals.
  4. Secondary (post-primary) TB — reactivation of latent bacilli (or exogenous reinfection) when cell-mediated immunity wanes; lesions develop in apical-posterior upper lobe. Necrotising granulomatous inflammation → caseation → cavitation into bronchus → expectoration of bacilli (high infectivity).

C. Gross & Microscopic Morphology of the Diagnostic Lesion — Tubercle / Cavity

Gross Appearance

  • Lung section shows cavity in apical-posterior segment of right upper lobe.
  • Cavity — round or oval, 1–5 cm diameter; wall is thick, irregular, grey-white; inner surface ragged with caseous (cheese-like) necrotic material; surrounding lung shows fibrosis & caseating granulomas.
  • Erosion of a pulmonary artery branch (Rasmussen aneurysm) → massive haemoptysis.
  • Erosion into bronchus → endobronchial spread (lower lobes), "staircase" or "tree-in-bud" pattern.
  • Adjacent pleura — fibrous adhesions; may rupture → tuberculous empyema or bronchopleural fistula.

Microscopic Appearance — Tubercle (Granuloma)

The diagnostic lesion is the caseating granuloma with the following structure (centrifugal layers):

  1. Central caseous necrosis — amorphous, eosinophilic, granular debris (named for the gross cheese-like appearance); acellular.
  2. Epithelioid cells — modified activated macrophages; abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, oval vesicular nucleus; arranged palisading around the necrosis.
  3. Langhans giant cells — multinucleate (20+ nuclei) giant cells formed by fusion of epithelioid macrophages; nuclei arranged in horseshoe / peripheral ring pattern at one pole.
  4. Lymphocytic rim — CD4+ T-helper cells (Th1) surrounding the granuloma; few CD8+ T cells & plasma cells.
  5. Outer fibroblastic rim — proliferating fibroblasts laying collagen → eventual fibrosis & calcification.

Acid-fast stain (Ziehl-Neelsen) — slender, pink, beaded, slightly curved bacilli (1–10 μm). Auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain — yellow-orange under UV.

D. Complications if Untreated

Local Pulmonary Complications (3)

  1. Cavity superinfection with aspergilloma (fungus ball) — haemoptysis; invasive aspergillosis.
  2. Massive haemoptysis — erosion of a pulmonary artery branch within cavity wall (Rasmussen aneurysm); life-threatening.
  3. Bronchopleural fistula & tuberculous empyema — rupture of cavity into pleural space; pyopneumothorax.
  4. Endobronchial spread → tuberculous bronchiectasis, lobar pneumonia.
  5. Fibrosis & volume loss of upper lobe, traction bronchiectasis, calcified granulomas.

Systemic Complications (2)

  1. Milliary TB & disseminated disease — haematogenous spread to meninges (TB meningitis), bones (Pott's spine), lymph nodes (scrofula), adrenal (Addison's), peritoneum, intestine, skin; in HIV — non-reactive miliary with little granuloma.
  2. Amyloidosis (secondary, AA type) — chronic active TB → nephrotic syndrome, hepatosplenomegaly, restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Clinical Pearl

Sputum CBNAAT (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) is the modern first-line test — detects M. tuberculosis DNA & rifampicin resistance within 2 h. Three sputum samples for smear microscopy. Treat with DOTS — 6-month course (2HRZE + 4HR) under RNTCP / NTEP. Drug-resistant TB — longer regimens (9–20 months) with second-line drugs; bedaquiline & delamanid for MDR-TB.

Classification of Kidney Tumours

GroupExamples
Benign — renal cortexRenal cortical adenoma, oncocytoma, metanephric adenoma
Malignant — renal cortex (adults)Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell 70-80%, papillary 10-15%, chromophobe 5%, collecting duct 1%, unclassified)
ChildrenNephroblastoma (Wilms tumour), clear cell sarcoma, rhabdoid tumour, mesoblastic nephroma
Renal pelvis & ureterUrothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, SCC, adenocarcinoma
Renal stromal / mesenchymalAngiomyolipoma, haemangioma, leiomyoma / leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, solitary fibrous tumour
Renal cystic tumoursMultilocular cystic RCC, cystic nephroma, mixed epithelial-stromal tumour
MetastaticLung, breast, melanoma, gastric
HaematologicalLymphoma, leukaemia, plasmacytoma

Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC)

RCC is the commonest primary renal malignancy in adults (~85% of all renal cancers); arises from proximal tubular epithelium.

Risk Factors

  • Smoking — most important modifiable risk (2× risk).
  • Obesity — ↑ oestrogen, insulin resistance; 1.5× risk per 10 kg/m².
  • Hypertension — independent risk.
  • Acquired cystic kidney disease in ESRD on long-term dialysis — 30× risk.
  • Hereditary syndromes
    • von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL gene, chromosome 3p25) — bilateral clear-cell RCC, haemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma.
    • Hereditary papillary RCC — MET mutation.
    • Birt-Hogg-Dubé — FLCN mutation; chromophobe RCC, oncocytoma, lung cysts.
    • Tuberous sclerosis — TSC1/TSC2 mutation.
  • Long-term phenacetin & NSAID analgesic abuse; asbestos, cadmium exposure.
  • Polycystic kidney disease — slightly increased.
  • Male sex (2:1); age 50–70 years; African-American ethnicity.

Pathogenesis

  • Clear cell RCC — mutation / loss of VHL tumour suppressor gene (chromosome 3p) → loss of regulation of HIF-1α / HIF-2α → constitutive upregulation of VEGF, PDGF, GLUT1, EPO, TGF-α → angiogenesis, glycolytic metabolism, oxygen sensing.
  • Papillary RCC — type 1 has MET mutation (hereditary), type 2 has NRF2-ARE pathway activation; chromosome 7 trisomy / 17 loss.
  • Chromophobe RCC — multiple chromosome losses; Birt-Hogg-Dubé association.
  • Acquired cystic disease-associated RCC — ESRD-specific subtype.

Morphology

Clear Cell RCC (70–80%)

  • Gross — solitary, large golden-yellow mass in renal cortex (upper pole > lower); well-circumscribed, pseudoencapsulated; haemorrhage, necrosis, cystic change; invasion of renal vein & IVC in advanced cases.
  • Microscopy — cords/nests/alveolar pattern ("small alveolar") surrounded by delicate vascular network; cells with clear cytoplasm (rich in lipid & glycogen, dissolved in processing), small uniform hyperchromatic nuclei; Fuhrman grading (1–4) by nuclear size & nucleolar prominence; WHO/ISUP nucleolar grading now standard.
  • Immunohistochemistry — positive for PAX8, CAIX (carbonic anhydrase IX), vimentin, RCC marker; negative for CK7.

Papillary RCC (10–15%)

  • Gross — well-circumscribed, tan-brown, friable, often haemorrhagic.
  • Microscopy — papillary or tubulopapillary architecture; type 1 — single layer of small basophilic cells around delicate fibrovascular cores; type 2 — pseudostratified large eosinophilic cells with nuclear pseudostratification; foamy macrophages in papillae, psammoma bodies, haemosiderin.
  • IHC — CK7 positive (type 1 > type 2), AMACR positive.

Chromophobe RCC (5%)

  • Gross — solid, tan-brown, well-circumscribed.
  • Microscopy — large polygonal cells with prominent cell membranes, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm with perinuclear halos; "plant-cell" / "koilocytic" appearance; binucleation common; Hale's colloidal iron stain positive (diffuse cytoplasmic).
  • IHC — CK7 diffusely positive, CD117 positive, E-cadherin positive; best prognosis of the three.

Collecting Duct (Bellini) Carcinoma (<1%)

  • Medullary location; infiltrating tubular & papillary; high-grade cytology; desmoplastic stroma; very aggressive.
  • Renal medullary carcinoma — sickle-cell trait carriers, very poor prognosis.

Spread

  • Direct — into renal pelvis (haematuria), perinephric fat, Gerota fascia, adrenal.
  • Venous — renal vein → IVC → right atrium (classic).
  • Lymphatic — para-aortic, hilar nodes.
  • Haematogenous — lung (cannonball metastases), bone (lytic, expansile), liver, brain.

Clinical Features

Classic triad (haematuria + flank pain + palpable mass) is now seen in <10%. Most cases detected incidentally on imaging. Paraneoplastic syndromes — polycythaemia (EPO), hypercalcaemia (PTHrP), Stauffer syndrome (non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction), Cushing (ACTH), hypertension (renin).

Clinical Pearl

RCC is the classic "internist's tumour" — diverse paraneoplastic syndromes, unusual metastatic sites (scalp, finger, vagina), and a long latency between nephrectomy and metastasis. Always suspect RCC in a patient with isolated metastasis to a strange site and a renal mass. Sunitinib, pazopanib, and immune-checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, ipilimumab) have transformed metastatic RCC therapy.

Atherosclerosis

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of large & medium-sized muscular and elastic arteries, characterised by intimal deposition of lipids, complex carbohydrates, blood and blood products, fibrous tissue and calcium — producing atheromatous plaques that narrow the lumen, compromise blood flow, and predispose to thrombosis, aneurysm and dissection.

Pathogenesis — Response-to-Injury Hypothesis

  1. Endothelial injury / dysfunction — chronic insult by cardiovascular risk factors (haemodynamic stress — hypertension; hyperlipidaemia — LDL; toxins — cigarette smoking; hyperglycaemia; homocysteine; inflammation) → impaired nitric oxide production, increased permeability, increased expression of adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1, E-selectin, P-selectin).
  2. Lipoprotein infiltration — LDL enters the intima through dysfunctional endothelium, undergoes oxidation (oxLDL) and glycation; small dense LDL is particularly atherogenic.
  3. Monocyte adhesion & diapedesis — monocytes bind adhesion molecules, migrate into intima, transform into macrophages.
  4. Foam cell formation — macrophages ingest oxLDL via scavenger receptors (SR-A, CD36, LOX-1) → become lipid-laden "foam cells" (yellow, lipid-laden).
  5. Platelet adhesion to injured endothelium → release of PDGF, TGF-α, & other factors → migration & proliferation of smooth muscle cells from media into intima.
  6. Smooth muscle proliferation & extracellular matrix deposition — SMCs synthesise collagen, elastin, proteoglycans → fibrous cap covers the lipid core.
  7. Plaque evolution — fatty streak (earliest, reversible) → fibrous plaque → complicated atheroma (calcification, haemorrhage, ulceration, thrombosis).
  8. Necrotic core formation — apoptosis & necrosis of foam cells, lipid debris accumulate in plaque centre — soft, acellular & pro-thrombotic.
  9. Plaque complications — thin fibrous cap rupture or erosion exposes tissue factor & lipid core to circulating blood → thrombus formation → acute coronary syndrome, stroke, peripheral arterial occlusion.
flowchart TD A[Endothelial injury] --> B[LDL infiltration & oxidation] B --> C[Monocyte adhesion & diapedesis → macrophages] C --> D[Foam cells → fatty streak] D --> E[SMC migration & proliferation] E --> F[Fibrous cap over lipid core] F --> G[Fibrous plaque → complicated plaque] G --> H[Calcification, haemorrhage, rupture] H --> I[Thrombosis → ACS, stroke, gangrene]

Morphology

Fatty Streak (Earliest — Children & Young Adults)

  • Gross — flat or slightly elevated yellow intimal streaks & spots.
  • Microscopy — subendothelial aggregates of foam cells (macrophages + few SMCs) containing lipid droplets; no necrotic core; potentially reversible.

Fibrous Plaque (Atheroma)

  • Gross — white-yellow, raised intimal plaque occluding variable proportion of lumen.
  • Microscopy — central necrotic lipid core (cell debris, cholesterol clefts, foam cells) covered by a fibrous cap (SMCs, collagen, elastin, few lymphocytes & macrophages).

Complicated Plaque

  • Calcification — makes artery hard, brittle; visible on X-ray.
  • Haemorrhage into plaque — sudden plaque expansion & luminal narrowing.
  • Ulceration / rupture — fibrous cap breaks; atheromatous debris embolises; thrombus forms on exposed collagen & tissue factor.
  • Thrombosis — partial or complete occlusion; major cause of acute coronary syndromes & stroke.
  • Aneurysm — destruction of media by atrophy weakens wall, causing dilation, especially in abdominal aorta.

Complications

  1. Acute arterial occlusion — myocardial infarction (coronary), cerebral infarction (carotid / cerebral arteries), mesenteric ischaemia, renal infarction, acute limb ischaemia.
  2. Chronic ischaemia — stable angina, claudication, mesenteric angina, renovascular hypertension, ischaemic cardiomyopathy, chronic kidney disease, multi-infarct dementia.
  3. Aneurysm — abdominal aortic aneurysm, popliteal, iliac; rupture — fatal haemorrhage.
  4. Dissection — intimal tear allows blood to dissect media (Stanford type A/B); sudden chest/back pain.
  5. Embolism — atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal emboli → "blue toe syndrome", AKI, livedo reticularis).
  6. Sudden cardiac death — arrhythmia from ischaemic myocardium.
  7. Heart failure — chronic ischaemic cardiomyopathy.
  8. Stroke & multi-infarct dementia.

Risk Factors

ModifiableNon-modifiable
Hyperlipidaemia (↑ LDL, ↓ HDL)Age (risk ↑ with age)
HypertensionMale sex (premenopausal protection)
Cigarette smokingFamily history (polygenic + monogenic FH)
Diabetes mellitusGenetic dyslipidaemias (FH, type III)
Obesity, physical inactivityEthnicity (South Asian ↑)
Hyperhomocysteinaemia
Chronic kidney disease
Inflammation (↑ CRP, SLE, RA)
HIV / antiretroviral therapy

Clinical Pearl

Plaque rupture (not slow stenosis) causes most acute coronary syndromes — a 50% plaque with a thin cap & large lipid core is more dangerous than a 90% fibrotic stable stenosis. Statins stabilise plaques by reducing lipid core, anti-inflammatory effects & thickening fibrous cap — benefits independent of LDL lowering. Aggressive risk-factor modification (lifestyle + statin + antihypertensive + antiplatelet + glycaemic control) prevents both initiation & complication of atherosclerosis.

Definition

Atherosclerosis (from Greek atherê — porridge, sklêrosis — hardening) is a chronic, progressive, multifactorial disease of intima of large & medium-sized elastic and muscular arteries, characterised by deposits of lipids, complex carbohydrates, blood and blood products, fibrous tissue and calcium — producing atheromatous plaques that obstruct blood flow and predispose to thrombosis, aneurysm and dissection.

Etiology — Risk Factors

ModifiableNon-modifiable
Dyslipidaemia — ↑ LDL, ↑ Lp(a), ↓ HDLAge (≥45 M, ≥55 F)
Hypertension (≥140/90)Male sex (until menopause)
Cigarette smoking (active & passive)Family history of premature CAD (M <55, F <65)
Diabetes mellitusGenetic — familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDLR, ApoB, PCSK9 mutations)
Obesity, metabolic syndromeSouth Asian ethnicity
Physical inactivity
Hyperhomocysteinaemia
Chronic kidney disease
Inflammation (SLE, RA, IBD)
HIV infection & antiretroviral drugs
Poor diet (trans fat, low fibre, high salt)
Psychosocial stress, depression

Pathogenesis — Response-to-Injury Hypothesis

  1. Endothelial injury / dysfunction — caused by hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, hyperglycaemia, homocysteine, toxins, infection, inflammation, shear stress. Even subtle injury impairs NO production, increases permeability, and upregulates adhesion molecules.
  2. Lipoprotein infiltration — LDL and especially small dense LDL, IDL, Lp(a) enter the intima, undergo oxidation & glycation; become immunogenic & cytotoxic.
  3. Monocyte adhesion & diapedesis — VCAM-1, ICAM-1, P-selectin, E-selectin expression on endothelium recruits monocytes; they enter intima, become macrophages.
  4. Foam cell formation — macrophages ingest oxLDL via scavenger receptors (CD36, SR-A, LOX-1) — unregulated uptake → cholesterol ester accumulation → "foam cells".
  5. Platelet adhesion — to injured endothelium releases PDGF, TGF-β, thrombin → smooth-muscle cell migration & proliferation from media to intima.
  6. Smooth muscle proliferation & ECM synthesis — SMCs switch from contractile to synthetic phenotype; synthesise collagen, elastin, proteoglycans → form fibrous cap over the lipid core.
  7. Necrotic lipid core — apoptosis & necrosis of foam cells releases lipid & cell debris, forming a soft acellular core that is pro-thrombotic.
  8. Neovascularisation — vasa vasorum ingrow; provide additional pathway for lipoprotein entry; source of intraplaque haemorrhage.
  9. Calcification — osteogenic differentiation of SMCs & macrophages; contributes to plaque rigidity.
  10. Plaque complications — rupture / erosion exposes tissue factor & collagen → thrombus formation → acute clinical events.
flowchart TD A[Risk factors → Endothelial injury] --> B[LDL infiltration & oxidation] B --> C[Monocyte adhesion & migration] C --> D[Foam cells → fatty streak] D --> E[SMC migration & proliferation → fibrous cap] E --> F[Necrotic lipid core & neovascularisation] F --> G[Complicated plaque: calcification, haemorrhage, rupture] G --> H[Thrombosis → MI / stroke / limb ischaemia]

Morphology

1. Fatty Streak (Earliest Lesion)

  • Gross — flat or slightly elevated yellow intimal streaks/spots; seen in aorta of children.
  • Microscopy — subendothelial aggregates of foam cells (macrophages, few SMCs); T lymphocytes; lipid-laden; no necrotic core; potentially reversible.

2. Fibrous Plaque (Atheroma)

  • Gross — white-yellow, raised, intimal plaque partially occluding lumen.
  • Microscopy — central acellular lipid core (cholesterol clefts, lipid debris, foam cells) covered by fibrous cap (SMCs, collagen, elastin, lymphocytes, macrophages, calcification).

3. Complicated Plaque

  • Calcification — brittle, hard artery; visible radiographically.
  • Haemorrhage into plaque — sudden expansion & luminal narrowing.
  • Ulceration / rupture — fibrous cap tears; atheromatous debris embolises; thrombus forms on exposed tissue factor.
  • Thrombosis — partial or complete luminal occlusion.
  • Aneurysm — medial atrophy & weakness; abdominal aorta most common.

Common Sites

  • Lower abdominal aorta (most common), coronary arteries, popliteal/tibial, internal carotid (bifurcation), circle of Willis, renal arteries, mesenteric arteries.
  • Lesions tend to occur at branch points & areas of turbulent flow (high shear stress).

Clinical Consequences

  • Coronary — angina, myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac death, ischaemic cardiomyopathy.
  • Cerebral — TIA, ischaemic stroke, multi-infarct dementia.
  • Aortic — aneurysm (rupture), dissection, atheroembolism.
  • Peripheral arterial disease — claudication, rest pain, gangrene.
  • Renovascular hypertension, chronic kidney disease.
  • Mesenteric ischaemia — post-prandial pain, weight loss, bowel infarction.

Clinical Pearl

Plaque rupture (not slow stenosis) causes most acute coronary syndromes — a 50% plaque with thin cap & large lipid core ("vulnerable plaque") is more dangerous than a 90% fibrotic stable stenosis. Statins stabilise plaques by reducing lipid core, anti-inflammatory effects & thickening fibrous cap — benefits independent of LDL lowering.

Infective Endocarditis (IE)

IE is a microbial infection of the endocardial surface of the heart — most often a heart valve, but may involve mural endocardium, septal defect, or prosthetic material. Characterised by vegetations composed of platelets, fibrin, microcolonies of organisms and inflammatory cells.

Classification

  • By duration — acute (<6 weeks; virulent organism, normal valve) vs subacute (>6 weeks; less virulent, abnormal valve).
  • By valve type — native valve (NVE) vs prosthetic valve (PVE — early <60 d, late >60 d).
  • By setting — healthcare-associated (nosocomial, non-nosocomial) vs community-acquired vs IVDU-related.

Etiology

SettingCommon Organisms
Native valve, communityStreptococcus viridans (30-40%), S. gallolyticus (bowel), S. aureus (30%), Enterococcus, HACEK group
Native valve, healthcareS. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Enterococcus, gram-negative bacilli, Candida
Prosthetic valve, early (<60 d)Coagulase-negative staph (S. epidermidis), S. aureus, gram-negative bacilli, Candida, Aspergillus
Prosthetic valve, late (>60 d)Similar to community-acquired NVE; viridans strep, enterococci
IVDUS. aureus (50-60%, MRSA increasing), Pseudomonas, Candida, Streptococcus; tricuspid valve
Culture-negativePrior antibiotics, HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Chlamydia, Tropheryma whipplei, Legionella, fungi, Brucella

Pathogenesis

  1. Underlying valve abnormality — rheumatic, bicuspid aortic, degenerative calcific, MVP, prosthetic, congenital (VSD, PDA, bicuspid). High-pressure jet of blood damages endothelium at site of impact.
  2. Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) — sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations form on damaged endothelium.
  3. Bacteraemia — transient seeding of NBTE with circulating organisms (dental work, IV cannulation, surgery, UTI, IVDU). Organisms must express adhesins (e.g. S. aureus fibronectin-binding proteins, FbpA, ClfA) and dextran (viridans strep) to colonise.
  4. Vegetation growth — platelets & fibrin layer over organisms → microbial microcolonies protected from immune cells & antibiotics; infection extends into valve tissue → destruction, perforation, abscess.
  5. Embolisation — fragments of vegetation break off → systemic emboli (brain, spleen, kidney, mesentery, limbs) — septic infarcts & mycotic aneurysms.
  6. Immune-complex disease — chronic bacteraemia elicit antibodies → circulating immune complexes → glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, arthritis.

Morphology of Cardiac Lesions

Vegetations

  • Location — typically on the low-pressure side of the valve: atrial surface of AV valves (mitral, tricuspid) & ventricular surface of semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonary).
  • Gross — friable, bulky, irregular, grey-yellow / grey-red masses; vary in size from a few mm to several cm; may extend onto chordae & adjacent endocardium.
  • Microscopy — amorphous granular eosinophilic mass of fibrin, platelets, entrapped RBCs & WBCs with colonies of bacteria / fungi within; underlying valve may show inflammation, necrosis, abscess; calcification in chronic lesions.
  • Difference from rheumatic (small, warty, firm, on line of closure) and NBTE (sterile, non-destructive) and Libman-Sacks (verrucae on both sides of valve).

Valve Destruction

  • Acute — perforation, ulceration, chordal rupture, valve prolapse, flail leaflet, acute regurgitation, heart failure.
  • Subacute — fibrosis, calcification, deformity, chronic regurgitation / stenosis.
  • Periannular extension — abscess, fistula, conduction block (aortic root abscess → PR interval prolongation).

Clinical Features

Fever (90%), new or changing murmur, splenomegaly, clubbing. Peripheral stigmata — petechiae (conjunctiva, palate), splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions (painless macules on palms/soles — septic emboli), Osler nodes (tender nodules on finger pulps — immune-complex vasculitis), Roth spots (boat-shaped retinal haemorrhages with pale centre). Heart failure, embolic phenomena (stroke, mesenteric, splenic, renal, limb), glomerulonephritis, mycotic aneurysm.

Diagnosis — Modified Duke Criteria

Major — (1) typical organism in 2 separate blood cultures; (2) echocardiographic evidence of vegetation, abscess, new dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or new regurgitation. Minor — fever ≥38°C, predisposing heart condition / IVDU, vascular phenomenon (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, Janeway), immunological phenomenon (glomerulonephritis, Osler, Roth, rheumatoid factor), microbiological evidence not meeting major. Definite = 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor; Possible = 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor.

Clinical Pearl

Treat empirically with IV bactericidal antibiotics for 4–6 weeks; organism-specific therapy guided by culture & sensitivity. Surgery indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, perivalvular extension, large mobile vegetations with emboli, prosthetic valve IE, fungal IE. Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures for high-risk patients (prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, cardiac transplant valvulopathy) — amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before.

i) Probable Diagnosis

Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) with cardiogenic shock and/or cardiac rupture / arrhythmic sudden death — sudden, crushing substernal chest pain radiating to left arm, sudden collapse on day 4 of admission — characteristic of ST-elevation MI with subsequent mechanical complication (rupture of papillary muscle, interventricular septum, or free wall) or malignant arrhythmia. The 4-day timing is classical for cardiac rupture.

ii) Etiopathogenesis

  1. Coronary atherosclerosis — chronic plaque in epicardial coronary artery (LAD > RCA > LCX).
  2. Plaque rupture / erosion — thin fibrous cap over lipid-rich core ruptures, exposing collagen & tissue factor.
  3. Platelet adhesion & aggregation — GP Ib-vWF, GP IIb/IIIa-fibrin → platelet plug.
  4. Thrombus formation — activation of coagulation cascade → fibrin-rich clot occludes coronary lumen → cessation of blood flow.
  5. Vasospasm — serotonin, thromboxane A2 from platelets aggravate occlusion.
  6. Ischaemia & infarction — within 20-30 min — irreversible injury begins; subendocardial myocardium is most vulnerable; necrosis spreads from subendocardium to epicardium (wavefront phenomenon) over 3-6 h.
  7. Reperfusion injury — if PCI / thrombolysis opens artery, oxygen-derived free radicals, Ca2+ overload, neutrophil infiltration cause additional damage; no-reflow phenomenon.
  8. Healing phase — neutrophils infiltrate (12-24 h) → macrophages (3-7 d) → granulation tissue (7-10 d) → scar (4-6 wk).
  9. Day 3-5 complication — necrotic myocardium is maximally soft (between coagulative necrosis & fibroblast proliferation); risk of cardiac rupture, papillary muscle dysfunction / rupture (acute MR), interventricular septal rupture (VSD), aneurysm formation, pericarditis, Dressler syndrome (immune-mediated pericarditis at 2-10 wk).
flowchart TD A[Atherosclerotic plaque in coronary artery] --> B[Plaque rupture / erosion] B --> C[Thrombus formation → complete occlusion] C --> D[Myocardial ischaemia] D --> E[Subendocardial necrosis → transmural infarct 3-6 h] E --> F[Neutrophil infiltrate 12-24 h] F --> G[Macrophage & granulation tissue 3-7 d] G --> H[Day 4-5: maximal softening] H --> I[Complication: free wall rupture, papillary muscle rupture, VSD, aneurysm] G --> J[Scar formation 4-6 wk]

iii) Laboratory Investigations

  1. ECG — ST elevation (≥1 mm in 2 limb leads, ≥2 mm in 2 contiguous chest leads), hyperacute T waves, Q waves developing in 6-14 h; new LBBB; reciprocal ST depression; arrhythmias (VT, VF, AV block).
  2. Cardiac biomarkers
    • Troponin I / T — gold standard; rises 3-4 h, peaks 18-24 h, persists 7-10 d (I) or 10-14 d (T). High-sensitivity troponin detects AMI within 1-2 h.
    • CK-MB — rises 4-6 h, peaks 18-24 h, normal by 48-72 h. Useful for reinfarction diagnosis.
    • Myoglobin — earliest (1-2 h) but non-specific.
    • LDH — rises 24-48 h, peaks 3-6 d (LDH1 > LDH2 — flipped ratio); historical.
  3. Echocardiography — regional wall motion abnormality (hypokinesis / akinesis / dyskinesis), EF estimation, mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture, pericardial effusion, LV thrombus, pseudoaneurysm).
  4. Coronary angiography — defines culprit lesion (TIMI flow grade); guides PCI.
  5. CBC — leukocytosis, neutrophilia (12-24 h), ESR raised.
  6. CRP — elevated, prognostic.
  7. Metabolic panel — glucose, renal function, electrolytes (K+, Mg2+), lipid profile, HbA1c.
  8. Arterial blood gas — hypoxia, acidosis in cardiogenic shock.
  9. Chest X-ray — pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly.
  10. BNP / NT-proBNP — heart failure severity.
  11. Coagulation profile — PT, aPTT, INR (for anticoagulation).
  12. Autopsy if sudden death — gelatinous, soft, yellow-tan necrotic myocardium with hyperaemic border; histology — coagulative necrosis, neutrophil infiltrate, wavy fibres, contraction bands (if reperfusion).

iv) Gross Changes & Microscopic Changes

Gross

TimeGross Appearance
0-12 hNo visible change / pale, mottled
12-24 hPale, soft, anaemic; hyperaemic border
1-3 dYellow-tan, soft, central necrosis with hyperaemic rim
3-7 d (sudden death window)Yellow-tan, softest, hyperaemic border; risk of rupture (day 4-5)
7-10 dRed-tan granulation tissue forms at margins
6 wk+White, firm, fibrous scar

Microscopy

TimeMicroscopic Findings
1-2 hWavy myocardial fibres; glycogen depletion; oedema
2-4 hCytoplasmic eosinophilia; basophilia; mitochondrial swelling; contraction bands (if reperfused)
4-12 hCoagulative necrosis; Pyknotic / karyorrhectic nuclei; early neutrophil infiltrate
12-24 hMarked coagulative necrosis; neutrophil infiltrate prominent; interstitial oedema & haemorrhage
2-3 dMaximum neutrophil infiltrate; necrotic myocytes lose nuclei; tissue soft
3-7 dNecrotic myocytes being removed by macrophages; early granulation tissue at periphery; risk of rupture maximal at day 4-5
7-10 dEstablished granulation tissue — fibroblasts, neovascularisation, lymphocytes, macrophages, pigmented haemosiderin-laden macrophages

Clinical Pearl

Day 4-5 post-MI is the "window of rupture" — necrotic muscle is softest, granulation tissue has not yet strengthened the wall. Risk factors for rupture — first MI, elderly, female, hypertension, no collateral circulation, delayed reperfusion. Suspect cardiac rupture in any post-MI patient with sudden electrical / mechanical collapse — emergency pericardiocentesis, surgical repair, and mechanical support are lifesaving if instituted immediately.

Definition (1 mark)

Malabsorption syndrome is a group of disorders characterised by impaired absorption of one or more dietary nutrients — fats, carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, water — across the small intestinal mucosa, resulting in nutritional deficiencies and systemic manifestations. It may result from defective digestion (maldigestion), defective mucosal absorption, or lymphatic obstruction.

Etiology (3 marks)

CategoryExamples
Maldigestion — luminal phasePancreatic insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, CF, pancreatic cancer); bile salt deficiency (obstructive jaundice, cholestatic liver disease, bacterial overgrowth, terminal ileal disease/resection, cholestyramine); Zollinger-Ellison (low pH inactivates enzymes); post-gastrectomy
Mucosal / absorptive phaseCoeliac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple disease, giardiasis, HIV enteropathy, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, radiation enteritis, Crohn's disease, short-bowel syndrome, amyloidosis, lymphoma, abetalipoproteinaemia, primary intestinal lymphangiectasia, mastocytosis
Transport / post-absorptive phaseLymphatic obstruction (intestinal lymphangiectasia, lymphoma, TB, Whipple disease); congenital transport defects — Hartnup disease, cystinuria, glucose-galactose malabsorption
Drug-inducedOrlistat (lipase inhibitor), cholestyramine, metformin, neomycin, colchicine, methotrexate, proton pump inhibitors (B12)
InfectionsGiardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium, Isospora, Cyclospora, Mycobacterium avium, HIV enteropathy, tropical sprue, Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei)

Logical Classification (3 marks)

  1. Pre-mucosal (digestive / luminal defect) — pancreatic insufficiency, bile salt deficiency, post-gastrectomy, Zollinger-Ellison, bacterial overgrowth (blind loop, scleroderma, diabetic autonomic neuropathy).
  2. Mucosal (absorptive defect) — coeliac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple disease, Crohn's, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, amyloidosis, lymphoma, radiation enteritis, abetalipoproteinaemia, AIDS enteropathy, short-bowel syndrome, congenital transport defects (Hartnup, cystinuria).
  3. Post-mucosal (transport defect) — intestinal lymphangiectasia, lymphoma, tuberculosis, Whipple disease affecting mesenteric lymphatics, primary lymphatic hypoplasia, right-heart failure, constrictive pericarditis.

Clinical Features (3 marks)

  • General — weight loss, malnutrition, growth retardation in children, fatigue, muscle wasting, muscle cramps.
  • GI — bulky, foul-smelling, greasy stools (steatorrhoea); diarrhoea, flatulence, abdominal distension, borborygmi, abdominal pain; increased stool frequency, oily stool difficult to flush.
  • Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency — vitamin A (night blindness, xerophthalmia, follicular hyperkeratosis); D (osteomalacia, hypocalcaemia, tetany); E (ataxia, neuropathy, retinopathy); K (bleeding, easy bruising, prolonged PT).
  • Water-soluble vitamin / mineral deficiency — vitamin B12 (megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy, glossitis), folate (megaloblastic anaemia), iron (microcytic anaemia), calcium & magnesium (tetany, fractures), zinc (acrodermatitis enteropathica, alopecia).
  • Specific to disease — dermatitis herpetiformis (coeliac); arthralgia, pigmentation, lymphadenopathy (Whipple); oedema (protein-losing enteropathy); aphthous ulcers (coeliac, IBD).

Laboratory Investigations (3 marks)

  1. Stool studies — 72-h faecal fat estimation (>6 g/day = steatorrhoea); stool osmotic gap; faecal elastase (pancreatic insufficiency <200 µg/g); faecal calprotectin (IBD); stool microscopy for ova, cysts, parasites; faecal occult blood; faecal α1-antitrypsin (protein-losing enteropathy); stool culture & toxin (C. diff); Sudan III stain for fat globules.
  2. Blood tests — CBC (anaemia — microcytic Fe deficiency, macrocytic B12/folate), peripheral smear (acanthocytes — abetalipoproteinaemia), ESR, CRP; iron studies; serum B12, folate; LFT; albumin, total protein; calcium, phosphate, magnesium, zinc; PT/INR (vit K); 25-hydroxy vitamin D; carotene.
  3. Malabsorption tests
    • D-xylose absorption test — distinguishes mucosal disease (low urinary D-xylose) from pancreatic maldigestion (normal).
    • Schilling test — vitamin B12 absorption (historical).
    • Lactose hydrogen breath test — lactase deficiency.
    • 14C-xylose / glucose hydrogen breath test — bacterial overgrowth.
    • Triolein breath test — fat malabsorption.
    • Selenium-75 homotaurocholic acid (SeHCAT) — bile acid malabsorption.
  4. Serology — anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG), anti-endomysial, anti-gliadin antibodies (coeliac); anti-mitochondrial (PBC).
  5. Endoscopy & biopsy — oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy with duodenal biopsies (D2/D3) for coeliac, Whipple, lymphoma, eosinophilic enteritis; capsule endoscopy & double-balloon enteroscopy for small-bowel lesions.
  6. Imaging — barium follow-through (smooth or thickened folds, strictures, diverticula); CT/MR enterography (wall thickening, lymphadenopathy, masses); abdominal ultrasound (pancreatic calcification, biliary obstruction); MRCP / secretin-stimulated MRCP for pancreatic duct.
  7. Direct pancreatic function test — secretin-cholecystokinin stimulation test (gold standard for pancreatic insufficiency).

Coeliac Sprue (5 marks)

Also called gluten-sensitive enteropathy or coeliac disease — an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by ingestion of gluten (prolamin — gliadin in wheat, hordein in barley, secalin in rye) in genetically predisposed individuals.

Etiopathogenesis

  • Genetic — HLA-DQ2 (90%) or HLA-DQ8 (5-10%); concordance in monozygotic twins ~70-80%; family history in 10%.
  • Environmental trigger — dietary gliadin; possibly infections (rotavirus, adenovirus 12) — molecular mimicry.
  • Immune mechanism — gliadin resists digestion → crosses intestinal epithelium (transcellular or paracellular, especially if tight junctions loosened by zonulin) → deamidated by tissue transglutaminase (tTG) → presented on HLA-DQ2/DQ8 to CD4+ T cells → Th1 cytokine response (IFN-γ) → epithelial cell damage, hyperproliferation, crypt hyperplasia, villous atrophy; anti-tTG & anti-endomysial antibodies (IgA) form immune complexes.
  • Innate immunity — IL-15 upregulation triggers intraepithelial lymphocyte cytotoxicity → epithelial apoptosis; refractory coeliac disease & enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL) may arise from these IELs.

Morphology

  • Gross / endoscopic — scalloped duodenal valvulae conniventes; reduction or loss of folds; mosaic / "cracked-mud" appearance; nodular mucosa.
  • Microscopy (Marsh classification)
    • Marsh 0 — normal.
    • Marsh 1 — increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs, >30/100 enterocytes); normal villi.
    • Marsh 2 — IELs + crypt hyperplasia.
    • Marsh 3a / 3b / 3c — partial / subtotal / total villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and ↑ IELs.
    • Marsh 4 — hypoplastic mucosa (rare, refractory).
  • Cytology — surface enterocytes lose columnar shape, become cuboidal; loss of brush border; increased mitotic figures in crypts.

Clinical Features

Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea, abdominal distension, anorexia in children. Adults — iron-deficiency anaemia (most common presentation), fatigue, osteoporosis, infertility, aphthous ulcers, dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy vesicular rash on extensor surfaces). Association — Turner, Down syndromes; type-1 DM; autoimmune thyroiditis; IgA deficiency; Sjögren.

Complications

  • Refractory coeliac disease (RCD type I & II).
  • Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL) — poor prognosis.
  • Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.
  • Osteoporosis, osteomalacia.
  • Infertility, adverse pregnancy outcomes.
  • Hyposplenism, sepsis (encapsulated organisms).
  • neurological — ataxia, neuropathy, epilepsy with occipital calcifications.

Clinical Pearl

Diagnosis requires both serology and histology — anti-tTG IgA is highly sensitive (90-95%) and specific (95-98%); small-bowel biopsy remains essential. Patient must be on a gluten-containing diet at the time of testing — gluten-free diet for 4-6 weeks can render tests falsely negative. Lifelong strict gluten-free diet is the only treatment; non-responsive coeliac disease warrants workup for EATL or refractory sprue.

A. Define COPD & Differentiate Emphysema vs Chronic Bronchitis (4 marks)

COPD — a common, preventable, and treatable disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases (GOLD).

FeatureEmphysemaChronic Bronchitis
DefinitionPermanent enlargement of air spaces distal to terminal bronchiole with destruction of alveolar walls (without fibrosis)Clinical — persistent cough with sputum production ≥3 months in ≥2 consecutive years
Anatomic siteAcinus (alveolar tissue)Large airways — bronchi & bronchioles
HallmarkLoss of elastic recoil → expiratory airflow limitationMucous gland hyperplasia, mucus hypersecretion → productive cough
Patient phenotype"Pink puffer" — thin, dyspnoeic, barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing"Blue bloater" — overweight, cyanotic, oedematous, somnolent
PathologyAlveolar wall destruction; α1-antitrypsin deficiency associationReid index >0.5; goblet cell metaplasia; neutrophilic inflammation
Chest X-rayHyperinflated, flattened diaphragm, increased AP diameter, bullaeIncreased bronchovascular markings, prominent hila
Blood gasesNear-normal PaO2 / PaCO2 until late (hyperventilation)Hypoxaemia + hypercapnia (chronic respiratory acidosis, polycythaemia)

B. Etiopathogenesis of Emphysema (5 marks)

  1. Protease-antiprotease imbalance
    • Inflammatory cells (neutrophils, macrophages) release proteases — elastase, cathepsin G, proteinase 3, MMPs (MMP-9, MMP-12).
    • Normally, α1-antitrypsin (α1-AT) inhibits elastase; α2-macroglobulin, TIMPs inhibit MMPs.
    • In smokers — ↑ neutrophil recruitment & activation, oxidative inactivation of α1-AT, increased MMP release → unchecked elastase → destruction of alveolar wall elastic tissue → permanent enlargement of airspaces.
  2. Oxidative stress — cigarette smoke contains abundant free radicals → deplete antiproteases (oxidation of methionine residue in α1-AT) → augment proteolysis; lipid peroxidation damages alveolar cells.
  3. α1-Antitrypsin deficiency
    • Autosomal recessive — PiZZ phenotype → severe early-onset panacinar emphysema, especially lower lobes, in non-smokers by age 40-50.
    • Gene on chromosome 14; misfolded Z variant polymerises in liver → hepatocyte inclusions, cirrhosis in children; in lung — unopposed elastase activity.
    • PiMZ — intermediate risk, exacerbated by smoking.
  4. Apoptosis / senescence of alveolar cells — endothelial & epithelial cell apoptosis, impaired VEGF signalling, accelerated ageing (telomere shortening) → loss of alveolar units.
  5. Autoimmunity — anti-elastin antibodies in some smokers; possible role of T-cells in disease progression.
  6. Risk factors — cigarette smoking (most important), indoor & outdoor air pollution, occupational dusts (coal, silica, cadmium), biomass fuel (chulha), childhood respiratory infections, asthma, low birth weight, genetics.

C. Morphological Types & Clinical Features (6 marks)

Morphological Types (by anatomical distribution within acinus)

  1. Centriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema — most common type; involves respiratory bronchioles (proximal acinus); upper lobe predominance; strongly associated with smoking; gross — focal black-pigmented enlarged airspaces around respiratory bronchioles.
  2. Panacinar (panlobular) emphysema — entire acinus affected uniformly; lower lobe predominance; associated with α1-antitrypsin deficiency; gross — uniformly enlarged, pale, dry lung; can be diffuse.
  3. Paraseptal (distal acinar) emphysema — involves distal acinus (alveolar ducts & sacs); upper lobe & subpleural & along septa; common cause of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults; associated with bullae formation.
  4. Irregular (paracicatricial) emphysema — adjacent to scars (TB, pneumoconiosis, healed infarct); not associated with airflow limitation.
  5. Bullous emphysema — large blebs / bullae (>1 cm) due to confluent alveolar destruction; may rupture → pneumothorax.
  6. Compensatory emphysema — overexpansion of remaining lung after surgical resection or collapse of adjacent lung.
  7. Senile (age-related) emphysema — uniform mild enlargement without wall destruction or inflammation.
  8. Interstitial emphysema — air in interstitium after alveolar rupture (mechanical ventilation, trauma); tracks along bronchovascular sheaths to mediastinum → pneumomediastinum.

Clinical Features

  • Symptoms — progressive dyspnoea (initially exertional, later at rest), chronic cough, scanty mucoid sputum, wheeze, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia.
  • Signs
    • Tachypnoea, prolonged expiration, pursed-lip breathing, use of accessory muscles.
    • Barrel chest (increased AP diameter), hyper-resonant percussion note, diminished breath sounds, distant heart sounds, expiratory rhonchi/wheeze.
    • Cyanosis (late), cor pulmonale, peripheral oedema, ascites (right heart failure).
    • "Pink puffer" phenotype — thin, dyspnoeic, near-normal gases until late.
    • "Blue bloater" phenotype — central cyanosis, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, polycythaemia, somnolence, peripheral oedema (chronic bronchitis predominant overlap).
  • Investigations
    • Spirometry — GOLD standard. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms COPD; severity by FEV1 (% predicted) — Gold 1 (≥80), 2 (50-79), 3 (30-49), 4 (<30).
    • Chest X-ray — hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, bullae, increased retrosternal air space, attenuated peripheral vessels.
    • HRCT chest — detailed emphysema distribution & type; bullae assessment.
    • ABG — hypoxaemia ± hypercapnia; chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation.
    • α1-antitrypsin level — for early-onset or lower-lobe predominant disease.
    • ECG, echocardiography — right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension (cor pulmonale).
    • 6-minute walk test, BMI, sputum, ECG.

Complications

  • Acute exacerbations (viral, bacterial, environmental) — common cause of hospitalisation & death.
  • Pneumonia, bronchiectasis.
  • Pneumothorax (especially bullous disease).
  • Cor pulmonale, right-heart failure.
  • Polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension.
  • Respiratory failure — type I or II.
  • Lung cancer (independent risk factor).
  • Depression, osteoporosis, frailty.

Clinical Pearl

Smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention — slows FEV1 decline by ~50%. Long-acting bronchodilators (LAMA, LABA), inhaled corticosteroids (in eosinophilic overlap), pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen therapy (LTOT >15 h/day for PaO2 <55 mm Hg — improves survival), non-invasive ventilation, and lung volume reduction surgery / endobronchial valves are tiered therapies. α1-AT augmentation therapy is indicated for confirmed deficiency with established airflow obstruction.
